She speaks of the departure and transfers of some Sisters. She is alone and very busy. She asks her to look into a basket that was sent.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I hear what you tell me about the Sister and I have received the letter too; how dreadful! I always told you so, and I was not wrong; well, send her to me at once, for charity's sake, have her leave with Sr. A. Battistina.1

  2. Listen, I am sending three religious to Genoa; among them there is an old one, not old, but a widow, whom I think would suit you well; you will see her; if there is one there, send me one.2

  3. The one you say should be sent to the house at S. P. d'Arena, I would say no, because it would be a mess if she were to tell the mistress something, being so cunning; whereas in Genoa she can do nothing; so send her to Genoa, where they are in extreme need;3 and as soon as you receive this letter of mine, send me the two sisters.

Goodbye in haste; I have so much work that you cannot imagine it; I do not know where to lay my head, it aches so; I really think it is the work.

  1. I am alone at the desk, so to speak, and it is 11 o'clock and I have already written 5 letters, all very long. What can I do? Sr. A. Carlotta I send to Poss's every day, where there were immense muddles, and so Sr. A. Benedetta goes round now to one [side], now to the other;4 in short, I am always alone at this sorrowful desk where all the good and the bad come down, but the good is a speck and the bad and the sorrow are a great deal, so that I see they are now consuming me.5 Fiat.

  2. May God give you strength and courage and pour His blessings abundantly upon you.

6. Listen, do me the kindness of tracing the mistress's basket, for I hear she has not yet received it and needs it badly; and also the things belonging to those two I sent you: inside there was a bundle meant for Anna Grasso.6 For charity's sake, see about sending it to us at once, because it matters a great deal to me.

Goodbye, your affect. [Mother]

I hope you have received my letter.

1 A letter had reached Sr. A. Innocenza from a customs guard. The Superior, worried about the matter because «this fellow» wrote to the Sister that he would come to see her in the hospital, sent the letter to the Mother, who decided to speak to the Sister and therefore had her leave together with Sr. A. Battistina Bertuzzi.

2 an old one, not old: she corrects herself: she is a widow. If there is one there: if there is a Sister to spare, have her come to me in Piacenza.

3 The one you say. Sr. A. Francesca wanted to transfer Sr. A. Domitilla, who was unwell, to the Institute at Sampierdarena; the Mother advises assigning her to the Genoa House.

4 Sr. A. Carlotta Biagini went to Poss's factory to restore good order; Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega saw to the running of the House.

5 all the good and the bad. The life of the Institute, with all its good and its negative sides, reached her through the correspondence.

6 Anna Grasso: one of the first five who set out with her for the foundation. She had left the Institute but remained on excellent terms. Cf. Lettere 1, p.523.

She encloses the dispatch note for a parcel sent to her and tells her that two Sisters are coming.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I enclose a dispatch note for you to give to Fr Antonio Accinelli; it is for the dispatch of 4 capons, two for him and two for you;1 and I let you know that on Thursday you will receive two Sisters.

  2. You will go and fetch them at the station; they leave here at 9, and I think they arrive in Genoa a few minutes after 4.

  3. Thank you for everything you sent me; in these Sisters' luggage you will find linen for the house, for the kitchen and the table.2

Goodbye, I am in a hurry

your affect. M. The Lord bless you all. Pray.

1 Fr Antonio Accinelli, thanking her on 8 January for having received them, wrote: «We are close to the turkey feast; I shall let you know whether it was good».

2 She had put kitchen cloths and table linen in the two Sisters' luggage.

Three religious will be arriving. She asks her to find out about the things she has sent.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Just a line; listen, you will receive three religious: two are for you and one for S. P. D'Arena, the red-haired one, who is from Ovada, Sr. A. Laura.1

  2. I hope the things belonging to the others I sent have arrived;2 and the basket of the mistress at S. P. D'Arena, mention it to the Superior, and the bundle that was meant for the Grasso girl.3 I am sure they will not have been lost.

Goodbye, I am tired

your affect. M. Rosa. God bless you all.

1 She sends three more Sisters, two for Genoa; one, the «red-haired» Sr. A. Laura Barberis, is for the Sampierdarena House.

2 Cf. L 6,6.

3 Ask the Superior, Francesca, for news of the things. Cf. ibid.

She introduces the two sisters she has assigned to the Lugo community, asking her to fit them into the school work. She speaks of the others who will be arriving for the new community at Mercatello and tells her what to ask the Archpriest about the teaching certificates needed for his school.

A.M.F.

My dear daughter,

  1. It is very late, but I do not want to send you the sisters without a letter from me. Listen, one will seem rough to you, but she reads and writes well; the other has a very good spirit and reads and writes well. Listen, if you see that they are not suitable, they will be changed; and if there is time they can be exchanged for those passing through;2 in that case you can also telegraph me, but I hope you will put them in order and will certainly make them useful. For charity's sake, dear Vincenza, because I would have no others.

  2. I have received your letters, but from today's, the last, I see that you have not received mine; I hope they crossed. Listen, they will also have paid you the fare for four sisters, as they had promised me; so on Monday, at the same time you arrived, the sisters will be at Castel Bolognese station; you will wait for them at that station and join them to go to Mercatello.3

  3. At Pesaro you will find the Archpriest, who wrote to me full of courtesies.4 Have him pay the fare too. Listen, for the certificates I shall send you that of Sr. Anna Tecla, who today came back to us,5 and you will withdraw the one belonging to the postulant already at Pesaro; you know whom I mean, the one I sent to Ferrara.6

  4. So see a little: this Archpriest makes so many re-

marks to me, wanting one with a higher-grade certificate,7 but I hope you will manage; if need be, tell him I shall send one; then withdraw Sr. A. Tecla's for me, and bring me the postulant's too if I have to send one of higher grade. Tell the Archpriest that I deliberately did not send him the other, because first I want to hear whom I should send, one of higher grade or of lower grade.

  1. I have written to the Count and I hope he will be pleased.8 Many greetings to everyone.

  2. When Mercatello is finished you can come back here. For the moment all is going well at Foligno, so you will go there when you have to take the religious for the Duchess; keep silent about it.9

Goodbye, it is too late. Yours on earth and in Heaven

affect. M.

1 The date is inferred from what she wrote in L 4,5: «The Sisters will be with you on the 7th of this month». Since she was to entrust this letter to the Sisters, it was undoubtedly written on 6 January.

2 Those passing through: the two Sisters on their way to Mercatello.

3 Cf. L 4, n. 7.

4 The Archpriest of Mercatello: Fr Pietro Tamagni. Cf. Lettere 3, p. 739.

5 Sr. A. Tecla Mazzini had left the Institute in November 1874 (cf. Lettere 3, L 367), but as she repented, the Mother accepted her again. She took the habit on 14 January 1875 and received a different name: Sr. A. Benigna.

6 On accepting the proposal to open the House at Mercatello, the Mother had sent the Archpriest the certificate of the postulant who was at Ferrara.

7 The Archpriest was asking for a «higher grade» certificate, that is, for teaching in the two upper classes of the elementary school: 4th and 5th.

8 To Count Raffaele Emaldi at Lugo.

9 The Duchess Agnese di Sora Piombino, who wanted the Sisters for the School she wished to open at Uppello (Foligno).

She warns her against pride, showing her the spiritual harm it does, and urges her to watch and pray, as Jesus teaches us.

A.M.F.

My dear daughter,

  1. I am writing to you again to let you know that that religious, to explain myself better, the one with the mole, has a petticoat; you will see it; have her take it off; mind you remove the red from it. For pity's sake, tell the superior to keep her under an iron hand; she is very [untaught] and still needs instruction in the Rules and in our life.1

  2. You will have received my letter which I sent you by post; having forgotten to hand it over, I sent it to you by post.2

  3. Do not grow proud on reading your mother's letter because of the praise she gives you. If we have anything good, it is God; we have nothing but wretchedness and sins; we are as ugly as pigs.3 Away with the world and its illusions; only one thing remains for eternity: the good we may do in this life with the help of God the Father; everything else ends up consumed with the earth and lost in the dust and the worms.4

  4. Humility! which we have not yet learned, and it seems that [pride] sprouts in our breast like a worm that is always gnawing; and blessed are those souls who have managed to drive this creature from its nest. Even then they must always labour to stay on guard so that it does not build its nest again, because it is always prowling and its one intention and effort is to achieve its purpose. Alas! [What can we do] but watch, as our master Jesus teaches us: «Watch and pray, if you do not want to fall into temptation»! So, my daughter, let us do it!5

  1. Listen, you know that I have no other treasure than prayer; from it

I have everything, and with it I obtain all my courage; one day we shall find our labours at the throne of God the Judge, and they will defend us from falling headlong into the abyss as we deserve.

Goodbye, greet them all for me, and believe me, on earth and in Heaven, yours more than anyone's

affect. M. Rosa

1 The religious with the mole (evidently she could not remember her name at that moment) has a petticoat (falda) edged in red; she is to have the coloured edging removed, and moreover she is to urge the Superior to guide her firmly (keep her under an iron hand), as she is not sufficiently prepared for religious life and still needs instruction in the Rules.

2 My letter which I sent you by post: it is L 9.

3 Do not grow proud... we are as ugly as pigs. Strong, incisive expressions in their realistic crudeness.

4 The eschatological vision of life and the clear Gospel teaching are always present in M. Rosa: Mt 16,26.

5 Humility requires constant asceticism: rising by lowering oneself, turning in continual prayer to Jesus the master.

She has already spoken to him of a young man needing lodging. She is anxious that he be helped, for good reasons.

A.M.F. My Father,

  1. I have received the letter and the box; thank you for everything, and may St Anne repay you; I tell her so every day.1

  2. Listen, I should like a favour, but you must speak to me frankly and as a true friend. You know that little Priest I wrote to you about, who would be coming to take his examinations there;2 I should like to know whether you could lodge him; I would have the Superior in Trastevere give him his meals;3 but you must tell me frankly if it is too much trouble for you; say exactly how you feel. In that case I shall think of turning to others to see whether I can find a room free of charge.

  3. Answer me at once, because it matters to me. You must know that this Priest is a great concern of mine, and when you know the reasons you will say I am right.4

  4. Listen, I seem to hear you say: «The mother is always up to something; she hasn't enough of her own, she goes looking for new ones!» Ah! My Father! The Charity that governs me never says enough; but it can tell you that it is stronger than my strength, since it is in my very depths that it does violence.5

Burn, burn this monster of a letter of mine, and believe me ever your poor

Sister Anna Rosa Gattorno

1 In his letter of 3 January he tells her he has sent a box containing 38 crucifixes, sweets as an Epiphany («Befana») present, and also lemons and oranges received from Sr. A. Domenica Marchesini.

2 She had written to him on 22 December 1874. Cf. Lettere 3, L 388.

3 The superior of the House in Trastevere, Piazza S. Agata, was Sr. A. Domenica Marchesini.

4 This Priest is a great concern of mine: Fr Giovanni Boffetti had warmly recommended the deacon to her, intending to entrust him with the task of teacher and formator of the young men wishing to join the Congregation of the Sons of Saint Anne that he meant to found. M. Rosa longed to see this work, the male branch of the Daughters of Saint Anne, come into being: this Priest (he was still a deacon) is a great concern of mine. The young man was ordained in his own diocese of Novara. Cf. L Giovanni Boffetti to M. Rosa, 26.2.78.

5 Charity... does violence. She feels it alive in her inmost being, the bursting dynamism of the charism that was to extend into the male branch of the FSA Institute.

The Count is not happy with the new Sisters. She agrees to withdraw one and decides that she should go to Mercatello. To Lugo she will send another Sister who will be the new Superior, replacing Sr. A. Edvige, whom she assigns to Mercatello.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Yesterday I received a telegram from the Count telling me that they do not like the two I sent them.1 Listen, [about] one he may be right, but about the other he is wrong.

  2. So the one from Rome must stay, and the one with the mole will serve as cook at Mercatello, and to you there I shall send another with whom they will be pleased, namely Sr. A. Innocenza.2

  3. You will take the Superior, Sr. A. Edvige, with the one with the mole, to Castel Bolognese, and so the Superior3 will take Sr. A. Innocenza and you will take away the one with the mole; the other is to stay. The post is leaving, enough; I am

Affect. M. R.

1 Cf. L4,5; L9.1.

2 Sr. A. Innocenza Bergamini.

3 She does not write the name of the new Superior for Lugo; perhaps she meant to assign Sr. A. Battistina Bertuzzi instead of sending her to Mercatello. The Mother had considerable doubts about Edvige's success (cf. L 4), and so she would have liked to replace her, but fortunately she did not. Cf. L 13,1.

Further arrangements regarding the Sisters to be assigned to Lugo and Mercatello. She is to urge the Superior at Lugo to keep an eye on the two Sisters arriving and help them become true religious.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. This morning I wrote to you,1 and now again; I hope you receive this in time; meanwhile do this: you will no longer take the Superior with you, but the two they want me to remove,2 and so one of them, the one from Rome, you will send back down alone, because I do not think it good to take her to Mercatello.3

  2. So at that station you will find the two who are to go to Lugo, and you will keep the one with the mole as cook for Mercatello, with Sr. A. Battistina as Superior and Sr. A. Carmelina as teacher, and you will tell them that [for] the other teacher I am waiting to know how I should send her, whether of lower grade, as is the certificate they have, or else they will return me the lower-grade certificate and I shall send them the higher-grade one; tell the Archpriest so.4

  3. If Sr. A. Alberta could be here by Monday morning I should be glad; see what you can do. The two for there will be Sr. A. Innocenza and Sr. A. Stanislaa, who will do their year of training.5

  4. Listen, for charity's sake, tell her to keep them in sight, for charity's sake, and not leave them alone; urge her to watch over them, for they are two girls who need supervision; I add nothing more, because I want to post this.

Yours in haste

Affect. M. Rosa

1 It is L 12.

2 She has changed her mind about what she said in the previous letter. She agrees to transfer the two Sisters from Lugo.

3 She will have Sr. A. Alberta Capoferri leave for Piacenza.

4 Sr. A. Battistina Bertuzzi was the Superior of the Mercatello community and Sr. A. Carmelina Carretta the teacher; before sending the other teacher she was awaiting clarification from Archpriest Tamagni. Cf. L 9,4 and the related note.

5 The two for Lugo, Sr. A. Innocenza Bignamini and Sr. A. Stanislaa Vignoli, were students; they had to do their year of training before the certificate examinations. They needed formation, being too young. The Superior was to follow them with attention and care.

She gives her opinion about the Vernengo Sisters. She is pleased with how the House is going.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received your letter; it consoles me greatly to hear the good news of the House, and that you are paying off the bills.1

  1. The answer you gave the Vernengo sister is from God, because it is inspired by Him; you could not have said anything better.2 Firmly: I do not allow them ever to go out alone; as long as they wear the habit they must respect it. That is how it must be done, without pity; in our Rules no exception of any kind is to be made. Let them turn to the major Superiors, who will answer them as is fitting.

  2. For the rest I am pleased and I bless you a thousand times, that it may give you strength and encouragement.

Your Affect. M. R.

P.S. Mind you send me the accounts for the year 1874.

1 The letter is dated 6 January. One of the consoling items of news: she is paying off the debts.

2 The Vernengo sisters, Sr. A. Concetta and Sr. A. Giuseppa, had been accepted exceptionally on condition that they lived in the Sampierdarena House, because Giuseppa was ill and her Sister had to look after her. They undertook to pay a monthly annuity on the property that formed their dowry. Cf. Lettere 2, p. 708. The answer you gave... Sr. A. Concetta wanted to go out alone, and the Superior had told her she was bound to observe the Rule as long as she wore the habit of Saint Anne. The two Sisters, already resolved to go back home, left the Institute on 15 May 1875. Cf. L Accinelli to M. Rosa of that date.

She hopes they will be pleased at Lugo with the two new Sisters. She is to send off the other, who is unsuitable. She tells her that on her return from Mercatello she must go to Lugo for at least two days and then to Foligno.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. Just a line, because it is late and I am so busy that you certainly could not believe it. So I hope these two I am sending for Lugo will be liked, and also these three you will take to Mercatello.2 I am waiting for that one on her own whom I told you to send me, who seems half dead. I would have said it would go like this, because I don't like her. Enough, now I have arranged everything and I hope there will be no more trouble.

  2. On your way back you will go to Lugo again and so see whether everything is going well, and you can stay there two days; and then, on your way here, you must go to Foligno; remember that I promised it,3 but I hope you will be quick at Mercatello.

  3. Goodbye for now; the sister will tell you by word of mouth many things that cannot be put in writing. Your affect.

[Mother]

If you run short of money, write to me in time and I shall send you some. I hope you will be here by the end of January. Yours for all ages. Amen, more yours than mine, and I your affect. M.

1 The date is clear from the context: she entrusts it to the Sisters, who were to leave on 11 January, cf. L 4,5.

2 Cf. L 12 and 13.

3 She had promised the Duchess Agnese di Sora to open a house at Uppello, a hamlet of Foligno. Cf. L 9, n. 9.

Motherly advice. He is to beware of bad companions and look for work. He should join the Society of St Vincent and pray to the Lord with trust.

A.M.F. My Alessandro,

  1. I have received your letter and, listen, you certainly cannot imagine how much pain it caused me; I do not allow it and I shall never consent.1 Listen, try to be a good Christian, keep away from bad companions, and go home early.2

  2. For charity's sake, Alessandro, I beg you to leave those companions; when they tell you that I cannot keep you, answer that so far you have been a burden to no one but your mother, and that it will always be so.3

  3. I hope the job will come. Try to go and see Magnini4 often, and you will see that by pestering him you will get it.

  4. Oh! how glad I should be if you gave everyone a slap in the face by enrolling in the Society of St Vincent!5

  5. You must know that I belonged to it for a long time, and you will see that the Lord will grant you the graces you desire.

  6. I have no one in the world but my God; from Him I have and obtain everything; see what graces He continues to give me! Ah! my dear Alessandro, listen, turn to the Lord and you will have everything.6

  7. I await a letter from you telling me that you have enrolled; what a consolation to see my son going to the poor to help them! The consolation would be too great for me! It depends on you. Yours, because it is late, most affect.

M. R.

1 Alessandro's letter has not been preserved. He had certainly [expressed] to her his wish to emigrate to America. Cf. L 22,4.

2 The young man was twenty and could not find work. Lo e[...] Fr Accinelli, with whom he did not get on, because he reproached him, [...]ly for coming home after midnight, and was very strict with him

Accinelli to M. Rosa of 19.1.1875. Sr. A. Francesca too, in spite of herself

[...]sing Alessandro, gave her far from good news.

3 You have been a burden to no one: you have not been dependent on anyone

4 A gentleman in Genoa to whom they had turned to obtain a job for Alessandro. Cf. L 22,3.

5 In that seriously Christian setting committed to charity he would have received the help he needed: good companions, excellent advice, an open and free field for the benefit of the poor. In this way he would have recovered and channelled towards good his gifts and his goodness of heart, and been tempered and morally strengthened. He would thus have given everyone a clear lesson (a slap in the face).

6 Turn to the Lord and you will have everything. In this pleading admonition to her son is contained her act of faith in the power of prayer, according to Jesus' promise. Cf. Mt 21,22; 7,7; Mk 11,24.

She asks her to buy and send booklets of the «Crown of the Lord».

A.M.F.

[Dear daughter,]

  1. I should like you to do me the kindness of buying me 24 Crowns of the Lord.2 You know, the little booklets you sent me once before, which Fasicorno sells near San Matteo.

  2. Put them all together and then, with a piece of paper cut like a band, put it round the middle and with another form a cross, with two (illegible word).3 I hope you will send them soon.

Goodbye, your M.

1 The date is inferred from Sr. A. Santina's L to M. Rosa of 11 January 1875, with the message: «Mother, you will receive the crowns of the Lord, which I am now going to buy».

2 Crown of the Lord. A devotional «practice» made up of 33 short reflections on the passion of Jesus, followed by the Our Father and other prayers.

3 She explains how to wrap the booklets for posting.

She advises how to handle a school problem and how to behave with the school Inspector.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I have just received yours with the register enclosed; listen, these threats are of no account for us, because with God's help we do what we can in all conscience.1

  2. To find out where they live, ask the girls themselves, as we do here; only I am writing to you as we have written too.2 For the rest, once you have done it, go to the Inspector, you and the Superior, not the lay teacher, and ask him with humility and gentleness whether it is all right, saying that if it is not right you will do it again, and that he should come and see how the schools are going and whether they please him; that you are not satisfied unless He comes and assures you of it.3

  3. In this way you will be sure of not being in breach, and if he finds anything that is not right you will do it again. Send me news at once of what he told you, because I am anxious.

  4. If I need to send Sr. A. Vincenza I shall send her; it certainly makes me fear there is something behind it, since this one is made differently from those I have received.4 See that nothing happens. Goodbye in haste, your Affect.

M. Rosa

1 The day before, the Sister had sent her the class register for her to examine against a recent circular from the School Board, also enclosed for her to see, which gave orders on how registers were to be filled in. The Mother reassures her: these threats are of no

Ai

account, they are not meant for us, who do everything in all conscience.

2 She is to ask the girls their address; that is what is done in Piacenza.

3 Further advice: to submit the register to the Inspector and invite him to visit the school.

4 She wants to know the Inspector's opinion; she fears there may be something to clear up, because the Ferrara circular is different from the one she received for the school in Piacenza.

Worried about her health, she urges her to take care of herself. She is waiting for her. Afterwards she must go to Uppello.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I received yours through Sr. A. Alberta,1 and I hear that your voice is still weak. Alas! how I suffer over it, you certainly cannot imagine. If it is true2 that you love me and want to be a comfort to me, take care of yourself, for charity's sake.

  2. I forgot to send you the privileges for the chapel; I am sending them to you at once.3

  3. Take care of yourself; I cannot wait for you to be finished,4 so that you can come and rest, because it is certainly nothing but tiredness.

  4. They are expecting you at Uppello, but keep silent, because you know why.5 Enough, I shall tell you many things by word of mouth.

Your affect. [Mother]

5. Carlottina is in bed with a swollen face and last night she gave us all a bad time. Enough, she is sleeping now and I hope it will be nothing much,

your Affect. M.

1 Sr. A. Alberta Capoferri, who had returned to Piacenza from Lugo. Cf. L 13, n. 3.

2 If it is true.

3 / «privilegi»: the copy of the faculties granted by Pius IX to M. Rosa in 1866 for the chapels of the Institute then to be founded, namely: to set up a private oratory in the houses and reserve the Blessed Sacrament, etc. These faculties were, however, subject to the permissions of the Bishops and Ordinaries of the respective places. AFSA SS F-1,81.

4 che sii lesta, that you have finished.

5 Cf. L 15, n. 3.

Worried by her silence, she asks her to write. She has appointed Sr. A. Carlotta Biagini superior of the Mother House.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I am in a state because I have no letters from you; I do not know what to think; that you are ill, I say to myself: she would have had someone else write; in short, I think all sorts of things.1 Put me out of my anxiety.

  2. I enclose F. 5, which you gave Sr. A. Albertina and which they would not take here, as they are from your part of the country; so try to spend them, and don't keep any, because they are not accepted here.2

  3. Today I made Sr. A. Carlotta Superior here; because, as we must leave when you come, it was certainly not advisable to wait and appoint her when we were on the point of departure.3 I am sure you will be pleased.

  4. Ah! what a sad day! Sr. A. Benedetta did nothing but cry; and I, with my temperament; how painful to see someone cry for no reason. Enough, you will hear by word of mouth what mercy of God it is that allows this for my sins.

Yours in haste affect. M. R.

1 Her concern is justified: Sr. A. Vincenza, of very delicate health, is wearing herself out opening the houses. The Mother has learned that she has lost her voice, but Vincenza reassures her that she is well: «At Lugo my voice was weak because I was teaching; I had a class of 50 unruly girls and the classes to organise as well» (L 14.1.1875).

2 Sr. A. Vincenza had given Sr. A. Albertina Capoferri (cf. L 19, n. 1) 5 francs, which had been refused in Piacenza as not valid. She is to spend them herself.

3 Sr. A. Carlotta Biagini. She appointed her without consulting her because, as she (the Mother) was to leave Piacenza on Vincenza's return, it was not advisable to give her the office on the eve of departure.

She has received her first letter. She is to withdraw the certificate that is not needed and send it to her.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. At last I have received yours, which I see is the first you have written me, because you give me the first news of the journey and of the welcome you received.1

  2. Listen, for charity's sake withdraw the teacher's certificate, you know she is now at Ferrara, because it is no longer any use to you, unless I send her; well, we shall see; this is more than the 4th time.2

  3. Believe me, my dear, the work increases beyond measure; I really wish you could [...].3 I must stop, otherwise, you certainly cannot believe it, this letter will never go.4

Your affect. M. R.

1 The letter the Mother speaks of has not been preserved.

2 For the certificate cf. L 9, 4 and the related notes. This is more than the fourth time I have mentioned it.

3 She leaves the sentence unfinished.

4 I must stop... letter. I must stop, otherwise (you certainly cannot believe it) this letter will never go; so much work takes up all her time.

She feels the distance and needs help, but finds everything in God. She urges her to love Him. She asks her to look into Alessandro's situation and find out from mamma Adelaide whether it is true that they want to send him to America. She is also to try to speak with Signora Morando.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. You tell me you have no letters from me; what can I do, my dear, I am so busy that I do not know what to do first.1 If you knew

[h]ow this morning, at a moment of certain complications, I wished you were near me. Enough, so God wills; you had spoilt me too much, and I took advantage of your charity and goodness, so now I am paying for it all; there is no longer any danger of my having someone to lean on.

2. But in God I find all I need. He makes up for the emptiness left by creatures. Oh! how good He is to me! Yes, I cannot help telling you with all the strength of my soul: «Love, love God and then you will have everything. The flesh groans under the weight of a prolonged martyrdom in this vale of sorrow and anguish; where does it find its relief? In that infinite Being in whom everything is found, because if the flesh suffers, the spirit rejoices, and so sorrow becomes sweet as honey».2

  1. Listen, if you could go to Genoa for a little to see how Alessandro is, and at the same time call on Mr Magnini, you know, that sick Gentleman we visited together, to see whether he has found anything yet for Alessandro; and also hear a little what Mamma says.

  2. Do you know what they have now got into their heads? To send him to America.3

Tell me, what do you think? How dreadful! Can God want this too? Ah! no, it is not because he is my son according to the flesh, but his soul, which is dearer to me than my own eyes! There, in that abyss of a thousand errors, there where every kind of unbelief is found, in short the beginning of hell for a poor young man who, with no experience of the world, must throw himself into it! Where! Alas!4

  1. Don't let it be noticed that I have spoken to you about it, but hear what she tells you, and then answer her whatever the Holy Mother puts into your mind.

  2. Listen, I have been told in a letter that a man fell from a window in your hospital; is it true?5

  3. Find out what is the matter with Signora Morando;6 I hear she is displeased, and it grieves me to hear she is displeased; if there is something, let her have it written to me and I will put everything right. It would be a serious matter now if she were to take offence.

  4. My God! how many troubles! For charity's sake, see to this at once, don't let days go by, because it could do harm; so I hope you will do it promptly.

Goodbye, yours for ever and ever

Amen affect. M. R.

1 You tell me. Sr. A. Francesca had written to her on the 14th: «For some days now I have had no news of you». And on the 18th: «...I do not know what to think, I am really worried; for charity's sake have two lines written to me, because I cannot be without news of you».

2 Loneliness, lack of comfort because of the distance of the daughters who with charity and goodness had supported and encouraged her. But in God she finds everything. She can say with St Paul: «As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing everything» 2 Cor 6,10.

3 Cf. L 16,1 and note.

4 a poor young man with no experience who must face a dangerous and hostile reality. Her fears were not unfounded. In Argentina Alessandro had to suffer a great deal and was forced to return to Italy, poor and disillusioned.

5 It is true, Francesca replies on 19 January; he was seriously ill; he had asked the Sister nurse to open the window a little because he could not breathe, and when the Sister went to fetch a cup of broth for the patient sharing his room, he made the senseless act. He died two days later. The incident had appeared in the newspaper «Il Balilla».

6 Signora Nina Morando, a friend of Mother Rosa and the Sisters and a benefactress of the Institute. She had been taken in as a guest at the Sampierdarena House, which she left in November 1876. Cf. L Accinelli to M. Rosa: 9.11.1876.

She speaks to him of a «difficult» young woman he has entrusted to her, assuring him that she will do her best to help her mend her ways.

Most Rev. Excellency,

  1. I beg your pardon for the mistake of putting someone else's letter in place of Paolina's; it grieved me greatly.2 Only the charitable expressions of your esteemed letter assure me of your indulgence.

  2. As for Paolina,3 Your Most Rev. Excellency may be sure that I shall do as you tell me, but I find in her such duplicity that it worries me a great deal. The kindness shown her is beyond compare, and unfortunately she is indifferent to it. May God hear our prayers and convert her.

  3. I cannot set out certain of her tricks in a letter, but if the good Lord grants me to be at Your Feet, I shall tell you everything freely and Your Most Rev. Excellency will know how to find the means to convert her truly; I am certainly not capable of it, lacking every virtue and all knowledge, a poor little woman with nothing good in her.4

  4. I cannot express to you how grateful I am for your prayers; I need them too much.

Deign to grant me your pastoral blessing while, on my knees, I declare myself with the highest esteem and admiration

Your Most Rev. Excellency's Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

1 The day is inferred from the Archbishop's L from Rome dated 16 January 1875, to which the Mother is replying.

2 The mistake was pointed out to her by the Archbishop, who returned the L from Sr. A. Filomena Pugnaloni addressed to a fellow sister, which she had enclosed instead of Paolina's.

3 Paolina, a young woman from Florence. Father Vincenzo Sallua had recommended her to M. Rosa on 7 December 1874 on behalf of the Archbishop.

4 The Mother thinks it will be hard to reclaim the girl, above all because she lacks honesty and is impervious to any kindness, having grown up in ignorance and without education.

She is glad they have a confessor; she is to tell Fr Accinelli and also ask him to look into the larger house. Advice about the nurses. She asks her to have the Sisters pray for certain intentions of hers.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I was glad to hear that the abbot has agreed to hear your confessions. I hope you have mentioned it to Fr Accinelli; so you can go to his Parish quite well, a few at a time, but let us hope that later he himself will say he will come to you. Accinelli must inform the Archbishop, otherwise there will be trouble later; enough, I am writing to him now;1 and I also enclose two lines for you to give to the abbot.

  2. See that Fr Accinelli takes up the matter of the house you say would suit you.2

  3. For charity's sake, try to ensure that the nurses observe the point about not separating; and take care not always to send the same ones to the place where the same four always go. Without changing them, you can split them up by having one lose two nights in a row and sleep during the day; in that way they get somewhat changed round. You understand me, don't you? If you have not understood, write to me and I shall try to explain in another way.3

  4. So I urge you to watch that they are not sluggish with the sick but try to be all charity, that they do not put on airs; in short, try to keep watch, get the most exact reports and contrive to know everything; and seeing you discreet, they will confide in you more and be sure that

you will not give them away to the sister accused.4

  1. For two days now I have had a certain fear about your house. For charity's sake, keep a hundred eyes open and watch the young ones closely so that nothing happens;5 in short, my daughter, I hope you will listen to my teachings and put them into practice.

  2. Have prayers said: first, that you may have the house you mention; second, that I may not have to take the oaths; and the other is the grace I am waiting for day after day.6 Oh! certainly, if the nurses did their works of charity well, I would obtain everything.

Goodbye, the Lord bless you and all the Sisters, while I am your

Affect. M. R.

1 This is the abbot of S. Cosimo. Being very busy, he had agreed to hear the Sisters' confessions provided they came to his parish. Fr Accinelli, informed of this, asked «the necessary permissions from Mgr. Vicar» and reported to the Mother in his L of 22 January 1875.

2 The house you say would suit better. The one they lived in on Via S. Donato was too small for the community of over 20 Sisters.

3 Observe the point about not separating. The Rule prescribed going in twos for home nursing and not separating (Chapter 8, 6 and 16). You can split them up by having one lose two nights in a row: the Superior replied that she had understood: when four sisters are assigned to nursing one patient, so that they change round and the same pairs do not always stay together, at the start of the rota one was to keep watch (lose) two successive nights (in a row).

4 That they do not put on airs: that they behave with dignity and seriousness; get the reports: find out in detail and precisely about the service and the nurses' conduct, and keep secret whatever one Sister may have told her about another.

5 I have... a fear: I foresee something sad. She is to watch the young Sisters, follow them and help them.

6 Prayer intentions: one, for the house she spoke of earlier; also that she may not have to take the oaths. Fr Angelo Ricchino, to settle the well-known lawsuit (cf. Lettere 1, p. 529), had requested a further sworn statement from M. Rosa in Court. The other grace is the official readmission of Fr Tornatore to the Institute. Cf. L 44,1; 47, n. 2.

Sr. A. Benigna, formerly Sr. A. Tecla, will arrive at Mercatello; she is to welcome her warmly and commend her to the Superior. Advice on organising the school.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. You will receive this letter of mine from Sr. A. Benigna; she was formerly Sr. A. Tecla, but you will embrace her and give her a thousand welcomes as if she were the dearest of all, and commend her warmly to the Superior;1 and see that you do not hand her certificate over to the Inspector, because I hope to change it soon, as I need it badly.2

  2. Try to keep her cheerful, and if Sr. A. Carmelina comes out with any of her remarks, tell her she must say nothing; she is not allowed to bring anything up again, or to mention the least of the things that happened.

3. The girl is in the fourth class3 and will help very well, and will pass as a postulant studying for her certificate, as indeed she is; do you understand? And you will bring me down the certificate of the lay teacher, the one from Ferrara.4 It seems to me that in this way everything will go well; and you can come down soon, because two days' stay at Lugo will be enough.

4. The girl will stay with Sr. A. Carmelina; meanwhile she will continue her studies, and I want her to learn enough to be able to take her certificate. So try to arrange to bring me down the Postulant's certificate. By word of mouth; we shall see each other soon. Remember that they must pay your fares.

Yours for ever Affect. M.

P.S. Tell Sr. A. Battistina to write to me often.5

Cf. L 9, n. 5.

She was sending her only provisionally.

She had assigned a Postulant to the house at Mercatello.

Cf. L 9, n. 6.

Sr. A. Battistina Bertuzzi, the Superior.

She must not complain if she does not write. There is only one reason: her many occupations. She holds her «ever close to the Heart of Jesus». She is to pray and persevere in her good resolutions. She awaits news of the coming audience granted them by the Holy Father.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I have received your letter and hear your complaints at not having letters from me in reply to yours; listen, the reason is my immense workload; I assure you I do not manage to do even the most important things; so when you see me slow to reply, you must think that it is the immense business that prevents me, and nothing else.1

  2. Know that this poor mother of yours always holds you close to the Heart of Jesus, so that one day she may have you with her for an eternity of joy; this is my wealth, this is all I think of giving you.2

  3. Yes, my daughter, if you persevere in your vocation, you will have what I tell you. Yes! I want it! And you assure me of it with the resolutions you have made, which were very pleasing to me to read. So take heart, let us put into practice what we say in words to our Dear Jesus.

  4. Tell the Superior that everything she says in her letter is fine; and so tomorrow, Friday, through you I shall receive the treasure of the Holy Father's Holy blessing; and I await a letter from you telling me in detail what he said to you and how you did, whether well or badly.3 Goodbye, the Lord bless you together with all the others.

your Affect. M. R.

1 The L she is answering is dated 17 January. The Sister fears that the Mother is annoyed with her and «displeased with her bad conduct». The Mother reassures her.

2 This poor Mother of yours. She was doubly a mother to her, for having taken her in as an orphan at the Mother House, she had followed her, fostering her vocation, and was still encouraging her by instilling in her the love of Jesus, her only wealth.

3 The Sister had told her that Mgr. Augusto Negrotto had visited the school and had given her the good news of their visit to the Holy Father, accompanied by him.

Alessandro is causing her great sorrow. She hopes to see her again soon. She thanks her for the oil she sent.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I have just finished reading your letter and hear about the man; but God permits it so that we may have ever more reason to humble ourselves; enough, let us leave everything to Him.1

  2. Do me the kindness of getting this letter of mine to Alessandro, and take good care not to give him more money than I have allotted him. Oh! the things he does! I assure you they are dreadful, and the more money he has, the more wickedness he commits. And this only feeds his vices. For charity's sake, give him nothing! How bad he is! Ah! it takes the life out of me to think of so many offences against God!2

  3. Let us hope to see each other soon; what can I do, I don't know what to say, I never get anyone I can count on; let us pray the Lord to send me some, and then I assure you I shall send you one.3

  4. I have received the oil, thank you; this blessed House is always in need beyond measure. Whoever is here4 really has cause for worry; one never finds the means to manage to do anything, being always without resources. Goodbye, that is enough for now. I am well.

God bless you, and believe me ever

your affect. M.

Cf. L 22, n. 5 Cf. L 16, n. 2

3 What can I do... send you one. What can I do (a stock phrase of familiar speech), I cannot find a Sister I can rely on (count on); let us pray the Lord to bring capable people into the Institute, and I assure you I shall send you one to replace you. Sr. A. Francesca was in very delicate health and overworked herself in the hospital, because of the great responsibility and the number of patients (50/54 a day).

4 Whoever is here: whoever is responsible for this House has worries and concerns because of the lack of financial means, which are very scarce.

She is to send off, if she thinks fit, the two Sisters she wrote about. She is to press Fr Accinelli to see to the house to be bought.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. How sorry I am that you keep sending me things; I don't want them, because grass is quite good enough for me.1 I hope you received those rags; but as soon as I can, which I hope will be next week, I shall send you a length of cloth from which you will make plenty of kitchen linen.2

  1. For charity's sake, if you think this sister you suggest sending here is careful, then send her to me at once. I hear there is one from Invorio who is threatening to leave. You can send her to me, so that when her parish priest comes he will take her away.3

  2. For charity's sake, keep after Fr Accinelli to see to the large house you mention. Let him buy it; it will be paid off little by little.4

  3. So take heart, my dear daughter; your letters give me real pleasure, bringing so much good news, especially that of Providence. May God continue to pour out His choicest blessings on this Community. Goodbye, your

Affect. M. R.

Pray and have prayers said.

Sr. A. Santina quite often sent her foods that might do her good, cf. L 7,3; 35,1; 91, n. 4; 112,1; 126,3.

2 Cf. L 7, n. 2.

3 A Sister from Invorio Inferiore. Her Parish Priest was Fr Giovanni Boffetti.

4 Cf. L 24, n. 2.

She advises her how to deal with certain Sisters and asks her to obtain medicines for the Superior at Terricciola.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. Listen, in strict secrecy: keep an eye on Sr. A. Prudenza. I know she stirs the sisters up, and takes the weakest aside and whispers to them so much that she makes them fall and lose their vocation. It will be better for you to send her to me at once together with the one you say was Sr. A. Stanislaa's companion.1

  2. I should like you to do me the favour of sending a box of Capuchin pills to Sr. A. Beatrice, who is unwell. The address is: Pontedera for Terricciola, Superior Sr. A. Beatrice. At once, because she needs them badly.2

  3. Tell Fr Accinelli too what I am telling you about this sister, whom I fear may team up with Sr. A. Natalina, because the latter, if she finds a sister to scheme with, is good at it; tell him that this sister writes in secret. Say nothing to them, neither you nor Fr Accinelli, because it would cause an upheaval. When she is here I shall put everything right.3

Greet Fr Accinelli for me. God bless you all; believe me

your Affect. M.

1 Sr. A. Prudenza Perfetti had received the habit on 14.1.1874. She wanted to hear them both and admonish them. There is no information about the one said to have been Sr. A. Stanislaa Vignoli's companion.

2 The Superior of the Terricciola House is Sr. A. Beatrice Merici.

3 Tell... everything right. It is well to warn Fr Accinelli about Sr. A. Prudenza's conduct and her fear that she may join forces with Sr. A. Natalina Bartoli. But they are not to speak to those sisters; she will deal with it in personal conversation with them and put everything right.

She gives some advice about the Community and urges her to go forward with courage to reach Paradise, where «the joy will be eternal».

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I have just received your letter and hear what you tell me about the girl; if you don't want her, send her away, call her relatives and hand her over to them; besides, if she does not pay, you are quite right. My God, what is one to do when there are no means!!1

  2. Then, as for the sister, take her to Genoa, and if you have more, take them all there; keep only those you need; I think 6 are enough; the others away. 6 including the Vernengo sisters, because I cannot see that this house needs more.2

  3. As for the money, you could tell her that as soon as you receive the girls' quarterly fees you will pay her; I shall send you some as soon as I can; I wish it could be today.3

  4. So take courage, don't lose heart, for charity's sake; we must be strong and never be cast down. Don't you know that after the storm comes fine weather? So after suffering come consolations. Courage, for when we reach paradise we shall suffer no more, but rejoice for an eternity of happiness. Come, my dear daughter, the exile of this earth is short, but the joy will be eternal.4

I await a letter in which I can see you much revived. Goodbye, the Lord bless you, and

believe me your affect. M. Rosa

1 Your letter... means. The L the Mother refers to is missing, so no further information about the girl is available; if she does not pay... means. The Superior was short of money. Yet it is painful to have to send this poor girl away.

2 As for the Sister... more. Perhaps a Sister in poor health. She advises reducing the number of Sisters to the minimum needed. For the Vernengo sisters cf. L 14, n. 2.

3 The money to pay off the debts.

4 courage... courage... the joy will be eternal. A courage that does not let itself be cast down by obstacles and is nourished by hope in the superabundant reality of good in eternal Life. Cf. 2 Cor 1,5;7,4. ; iV4,13.

She urges her to call on Countess Trotti and asks for prayers.

A.M.F.

My dear daughter,

  1. Just one line, which I hope will arrive in time. Go, for charity's sake, to the C.ss Trotti and stay as long as she wishes;1 I shall not write at length because I shall tell you everything by word of mouth.

  2. Tell the Superior to pray for the lawsuit which is to be heard on 20 February, and for my grace,2 and now also for my poor Alessandro, who is so very, very ill. May God's will be done in him.3

  3. Oh! my dear Vincenza, always new sorrows and new crosses. Tell the C.ss that I am not writing to her for now because my poor head aches too much.

Goodbye, your Affect. M. R.

1 ...arrive in time: before she left Lugo to return to Piacenza. Countess Trotti, a friend of Mother Rosa, had placed her palazzo in Ferrara at her disposal for opening the Girls' Boarding School and School. Cf. Lettere 2, p. 708.

2 Tell the Superior of the Ferrara House, Sr. A. Filomena Pugnaloni, to pray for her intentions: the lawsuit, etc. Cf. L 24, n. 6.

3 She adds another grace to be obtained: the health of poor Alessandro, who is seriously ill.

She entrusts to her a girl who was recommended to her and explains how to treat her.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. Today you will receive a girl I am recommending to you, Paolina.1 Listen, I should like you to find a way of making her fond of you and keep her with you as much as you can; and if letters came for her, try to hold them back and do not give them to her, but send them to me; and so, if you could manage to make her a good Christian. At the rosary we keep her only up to the Salve Regina, and then she leaves;2 I commend her to you. I hope to send her things tomorrow, and a new dress with shoes too.

  2. I commend her to you so that she has no cause to be unhappy. You can send her, or better take her, to the hospital now and then, because that way she gets out a little.3 You can get her to help you in the linen room; here she was a great help; she sews very well.

  3. I enclose a letter for you to give to Sr. A. Laura.4 I want to hear that you are cheerful; I hope to send you a little money soon.

Goodbye. Greet Paolina for me and tell her I want news of her and she is to write to me soon.

Your affect. M. R.

1 The young woman had been recommended to her by Fr Vincenzo Sallua and Mgr. Eugenio Cecconi. Cf. L 23.

2 ...she leaves: she leaves the chapel, because the Rosary was followed by other prayers proper to the FSA.

3 ...si spazia: she goes out, takes her mind off things.

4 Sr. A. Laura Barberis. Cf. L 8,1.

Her presence is urgently needed at Terricciola. She is to go and, after advising the Superior, return at once to Piacenza.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I have just received yours and hear that I am still in time.1 Everything is ordained by God; I enclose the letter from the archpriest of Terricciola; go there at once and order her to have treatment and be obedient, for this is the one virtue we can have and must have as our emblem.2

  2. Oh! how painful, my dear Vincenza, to think that on every side [...]. Alessandro is just the same.3 Leave at once for Terricciola, and as soon as you have been able to put that Superior in order, which I hope will be a small matter, come, come, for there are urgent things. Goodbye, yours for all ages

affect. M. R.

1 From Sr. A. Vincenza's L she learns that she has had to delay her departure, putting it off to 31 January. She is therefore in time to tell her not to go to Ferrara. Her presence at Terricciola is more urgent, the Superior being ill. Cf. L 29,2. She has received a letter from the Archpriest, Fr Secondo Griselli.

2 Obedience, our one emblem, must be modelled on the obedience of Christ: Heb 5,8; Phil 2,8.

3 Unfinished sentence. Alessandro's health is unchanged.

She expresses her gratitude for what she has done for Alessandro and urges her to look after herself and send news of her health.

A.M.F. Dear Francesca,

  1. So great is my emotion in writing to you that my hand trembles as I think of what you have done for my Alessandro.1 I cannot hold back my tears, my God! What shall I do for this dear and unique creature so devoted to me? Could she give me any better proofs of love? Ah! no, more cannot be given.2

  2. Tell me, have you suffered? how is the cough? Ah! take care of yourself, for pity's sake; don't make me die of grief, because hearing that you are unwell is a pain I cannot bear. Let everything go, as long as your health is saved.3

  3. My daughter, or better, my beloved Sister, my only one, today I am expecting either a letter or a telegram. God grant there is nothing wrong, but I am very much afraid.4 I commend Paolina to the Superior, Sr. A. Elisabetta.5 Many greetings to Sr. A. Benedetta, and wholly united to my beloved Jesus I tell you that living and dead I shall be yours for ever

affect. M. R.

4. I am very much afraid, if Alessandro were to come, because of that woman you know about. I should be happier if he stayed near you, and I should like [...]. See what you can do; whatever you do I shall approve.6

1 Sr. A. Francesca had helped Alessandro with motherly, affectionate under-

standing and with advice; she was the only one among the people he had dealings with in Genoa to take his health to heart.

2 The Mother's gratitude is immense for the selfless love of her dear «Franceschina».

3 Take care... health. Expressions of unspeakable grief over the health of her daughter, or better beloved Sister, my only one.

4 She is waiting for news of Alessandro's medical examination and is anxious, foreseeing the worst.

5 Cf. L 32, 1-2.

6 It was said that Alessandro was involved with a woman. The Mother prefers him to stay at Sampierdarena. And I should like... she leaves the sentence unfinished. She will approve whatever Francesca decides.

She thanks her for what she sent through the Sisters and asks her to send two bunches of flowers.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I have received your letter and hear what you tell me about Providence.1 God be blessed! The Sisters arrived safely; I don't want you always to send me fish, because, you know, dear daughter, for some time it has not agreed with me.2 Thank you for everything; I am grateful for your thoughtfulness.

  2. Listen, I should like a favour: send me for Sunday a bunch of camellias, not too big, I am sending you the size, and also one of violets. I want no one [...]. Send them for Saturday so that they are here by 2 o'clock. I hope you will not forget.3

  3. Dear daughter, listen: one you did well to send, namely Sr. A. Costanza, but the other, if she has done nothing wrong, I would be inclined to send back again together with a strong, good one.4 Write and tell me whether I may send her, yes or no.

Goodbye, your Affect. M. R.

1 The letter of 31 January brought her good news. The Superior had not only bought and paid for flour and sugar, but had 30 francs left in the cash box.

2 Sr. A. Costanza Cenni had arrived from Genoa the day before, together with another Sister, as she mentions below in para. 3, and they had brought the fish sent by the Superior, as she usually did when the opportunity arose. Cf. L28, n. 1.

3 I want no one: an unfinished sentence follows. The flowers had been requested by a lady benefactor. Cf. L 40,1.

4 ...the other (Sister) if she has done nothing wrong: if she has not behaved badly and therefore need not stay at the Mother House for a further period of formation, she can go back to Genoa together with another strong, good religious.

Alessandro is ill. She explains what must be done to resolve problems concerning the school and the Community.

A.M.F.

Dear Vincenza,

  1. God wills that I end my days amid the bitterest tribulations. Alessandro, I fear there is no longer any remedy; he looks like a corpse.1

  2. I sent the telegram just now, having finished reading your letter; and you will already have seen what I want. Enrichetta can quite well go alone, and you can have the other fetched by someone the Count trusts.2 Then all will be well; don't worry, these are small matters and are easily put right; I am sorry that meanwhile you are slow in coming; for charity's sake, hurry, because I need you here.

  3. I want the name and surname of this Inspector at once, at once. Tell the Count that I am not answering his letter immediately because I do not feel very well, but he is not to worry, for everything will be put right.

  4. As for the Confessor, let them accept the Parish Priest; they must not offend the Vicar; do things in order and with prudence. Tell the Superior not to worry, for everything will be put right.3 The devil has a hand in everything. What patience, my God! You will have [received] all my letters.

I am in a hurry, your affect. M. R.

1 Alessandro was ill. The Superior, Santina, had written to her the day before in these very words: «Alessandro is getting thinner and thinner». He was visibly worse day by day. The Mother has every reason to fear that he has tuberculosis.

2 At Lugo — Vincenza wrote to her — she had found the Superior, Count Raffaele and the Emaldi family in a state because the school Inspector from Ravenna, on inspecting the school, had found a serious irregularity: there was no teacher with the regulation qualification to act as headmistress and teach the 4th and 5th classes. The Mother has decided the remedy: Sr. A. Benigna Mazzini, who holds the proper certificate, will move from Mercatello to Lugo, changing places with Sr. A. Enrichetta Salvatelli, whose qualification was sufficient at Mercatello.

3 The Superior, Sr. A. Edvige Moroncini, had been worried.

She says she is pleased with the transfer of a Sister from Mercatello. Alessandro is better and is lovingly cared for by the Colli family. She cannot accept the girl she mentions. She is to try to come back soon, because she will have to go with her to Genoa for the «Ricchino case».

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Today I received your dear registered letter with the certificate and the Contract with the Commission, and also the Archpriest's letter and Sr. A. Benigna's. Blessed be God, who does everything so well.1 I assure you I think it a very good thing to take that Sister away from Mercatello, because with the Carmelo sister she would not have been very comfortable; so everything has turned out for the best.2

  2. Now I am weighed down with a terrible anxiety because I see from your letter that you are not very well. For charity's sake, dear Vincenza, don't wear yourself out; take care of yourself and have treatment. You see, we already have cruel proofs of what it means not to want treatment.3

  2. L'Istituto è recentissimo, perché non ha che 9 anni di vita, e conta 31 case, senza quelle che stanno ora per aprirsi.

  3. Il nostro scopo è l'assistenza degli infermi a domicilio d'ambo i sessi, il ricovero delle pericolanti, come pure l'educandato civile. La scuola dei maschi dall'età dei 4 alli 11 anni; scuola femminile, ospedali di cui non solo la direzione ne abbiamo, ma la cura stessa, facendo agli infermi tutto ciò che fanno le basse inservienti, da cuciniere, non avendo nell'ospedale che qualche uomo onde faccia presso gli uomini quello che la modestia proibisce.

  4. Per ciò che riguarda l'accettazione delle Postulanti, si fa molta facilitazione riguardo alla dote. Non è così riguardo alla vocazione e salute, che di questo se ne richiede scrupolosamente le più esatte informazioni.

  5. È vero che si accettano anche delle vecchie,1 e queste però bisogna che sieno munite d'una dote secondo della loro età. Abbiano le fedi di battesimo, buona condotta, attestati del medico, che mai sieno state a servizio, così nemmeno fatto parte d'altri Monasteri.
